Period schedule:
  Row 1: 45 minutes × 9 periods = 405 minutes
Total: 9 periods · 6h 45min

periods.activity_title: Voices of the Harvest: Reading the Hymn Aloud

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.176): match each stanza's main idea to its stanza number.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the poem aloud while students follow in their textbooks (p.173–175), attending to the three distinct voices — Men's, Women's, and All Voices. Students track which deity each stanza addresses and note unfamiliar words.
Students re-read their assigned stanza in pairs, practising voice and emphasis. Brief whole-class sharing: each pair reads their stanza aloud and names the deity being praised.
Class works on “Let us discuss” (p.176): students write the stanza number that matches each given main idea, then compare answers with a neighbour before teacher-led confirmation.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's four-stanza structure maps neatly onto three elemental deities — Surya, Varuna, Prithvi — and a closing address to Brahma; establishing this structure during the first reading prevents later confusion about who is speaking. Watch for students misreading the archaic pronouns ‘thee’ and ‘thine’ as unfamiliar names rather than second-person address. Students who struggle with the stanza-matching task may be directed to re-read the opening couplet of each stanza independently.

periods.activity_title: Tone, Imagery and Poetic Devices in the Hymn

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.176): fill blanks on setting, tone, and capitalisation with bracket choices.
Let us think and reflect (p.177): identify poetic device in two given lines.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.177): find more word/phrase repetitions and note the poet’s purpose.

time_bands.activity: Teacher-led discussion of the poem’s setting and tone using the fill-in task from “Let us discuss” (p.176). Students choose from the bracketed options and justify their choices with evidence from the poem.

Students examine the capitalisation of ‘Hands’, ‘Heart’, and ‘Home’ in the final stanza. Class discusses why the poet elevates these ordinary nouns and what they signify about God’s relationship with the farmers.

Pairs identify the poetic device in each of the two lines from “Let us think and reflect” (p.177) and share their reasoning with the class; teacher consolidates by naming alliteration and imagery on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the poem aloud and mapped its stanza structure, students are ready to examine the language more closely. A common difficulty is distinguishing alliteration from repetition — remind students that alliteration is about initial consonant sounds while anaphora repeats full phrases at the start of successive lines. Students who finish early may begin the homework task on repetition in class.
materials: Textbook p.176–177 (Let us discuss, Let us think and reflect)

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.177): match lines to expressions and poetic devices (imagery, personification, metaphor).
Let us think and reflect (p.177): match Prithvi, Surya, Varuna symbols to their meanings.

time_bands.activity: Students complete the three-column matching table from “Let us think and reflect” (p.177) — pairing lines to expressions and labelling the poetic device. Pairs share answers; teacher draws out the distinction between personification of Earth as mother and the metaphor of Seed and Scythe.
Class takes up the symbol-matching task (p.177): students pair Prithvi, Surya, and Varuna with their symbolic meanings, explaining how the poem's imagery supports each match.
Brief whole-class reflection: teacher asks students to name one image from the poem that they find most vivid and explain why, drawing on the symbolic meanings just discussed.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem presents Earth as an ‘omnipotent mother’ and God as both ‘Seed and Scythe’ — students often identify the second as simile rather than metaphor; a quick check on whether ‘like’ or ‘as’ is present helps clarify this. The symbolic meanings of the three deities align with their natural domains (sun, rain, earth), which students familiar with Indian mythology may articulate well — invite those students to share contextual knowledge. Students who did the homework on repetition may briefly share two examples at the start to warm up the session.
materials: Textbook p.177 (Let us think and reflect)

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.178): four questions on Extract 1 (Surya stanza) — MCQ, fill-in, short answer.
Let us think and reflect (p.178–179): four questions on Extract 2 (All Voices stanza) — MCQ, true/false, phrase identification, short answer.

time_bands.activity: Students read Extract 1 (the Surya stanza, p.178) silently, then answer the four questions individually — choosing the correct option, completing the fill-in, writing a short answer on Surya’s role, and selecting joy or worship for the instruments. Teacher facilitates a brief comparison of answers.

Class moves to Extract 2 (All Voices stanza, p.178–179). Students answer all four questions, paying particular attention to the true/false on ‘Seed and Scythe’ and the phrase-identification question on timelessness and ineffability.
Teacher-led consolidation: students explain in one sentence why the final stanza is sung by ‘All Voices’ rather than a single group, connecting this to the poem’s theme of universal devotion.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked through the poem’s symbols and imagery, students are prepared for the closer textual demands of extract-based questions. A frequent error is interpreting ‘being’ as the physical body rather than total existence — prompt students to consider the pairing with ‘Lord of the Universe’. The chorus question (‘How do we know these lines are spoken as a chorus?’) is answered by the stage direction ‘All Voices’ — students may initially look for a grammatical signal instead.
materials: Textbook p.178–179 (Let us think and reflect, Extracts 1 and 2)

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.179): seven questions on the poem — short answers and extended responses.

time_bands.activity: Students answer the four shorter questions (p.179) on Varuna, the wealth of the valleys, the Earth as ‘source of manifold gladness’, and the offering of labours as tribute. Each student writes individually; teacher circulates.

Class discusses the two extended-response questions — why the poem uses three distinct voices, and how Naidu creates the joyous atmosphere of a rural harvest festival. Students share a point each; teacher builds a collective response on the board.
Students write their own answer to the final question — why the poem is presented as a hymn — using evidence from the refrain, musical instruments, and the collective voice of the community.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem’s layered structure — men, women, all voices — maps onto the Hindu concept of community worship; students who engage with this dimension write richer extended responses. The question on ‘wealth of our valleys’ expects students to identify the newly harvested crops, not metaphorical wealth — steer discussions back to the poem’s rural, agricultural setting. Tasks on the poet’s purpose for three distinct voices and on creating a joyous rural atmosphere are best handled as collaborative oral discussion before individual writing.
materials: Textbook p.179 (Let us think and reflect)

periods.activity_title: Farming Implements, Synonyms and Archaic Words

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.180): match farming implement pictures to uses and complete their names.
Let us learn (p.180–181): choose correct synonyms for underlined words using context clues.
Let us learn (p.181): find modern equivalents for five archaic words using a dictionary.

time_bands.activity: Students match the six farming implement pictures (p.180) to their uses and complete the incomplete names (sickle, scythe, plough, trowel, rake, spade). Teacher draws attention to the sickle-scythe distinction, connecting ‘scythe’ to its appearance in the poem’s final stanza.

Students work on the synonym task (p.180–181): they circle context-clue words or phrases in each sentence, then choose the correct synonym from the box — generous, help, brightness, indescribable, kind.

Students use a dictionary to find modern equivalents of the five archaic words — morrow, hither, quoth, betwixt, yonder (p.181). Pairs compare findings, then teacher confirms meanings and notes that the poem’s ‘thee’ and ‘thine’ belong to the same archaic register.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem itself uses several words from this vocabulary set — ‘munificent’, ‘ineffable’, ‘succour’, ‘radiance’ — so the synonym exercise reinforces active reading of the text students have already explored. Students may confuse sickle and scythe based on their similar shapes; the implement-matching task is a good anchor for this distinction. If dictionaries are unavailable for the archaic-words task, students may pool knowledge before teacher confirmation.

periods.activity_title: Listening to Paddy Cultivation; Silent Letters and Harvest Presentation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.181): number seven events in the correct order of paddy cultivation.
Let us listen (p.181–182): answer three MCQs on the paddy cultivation talk on second listening.
Let us speak (p.182): say aloud words with silent ‘n’ (hymn, column) and silent ‘b’ (womb, tomb).

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the paddy cultivation talk aloud (p.203) at a steady pace while students listen and number the seven stages — ploughing, puddling, sowing, transplanting, irrigation, harvesting, threshing, milling — in correct sequence on their worksheets.

Teacher reads the talk a second time; students answer the three comprehension questions (p.181–182) on the main soil-preparation step, germination time, and the reason for drying grains. Answers are discussed briefly as a class.

Teacher models the pronunciation of words with silent ‘n’ (hymn, column, autumn, solemn) and silent ‘b’ (womb, tomb, bomb, climb, comb) from “Let us speak” (p.182). Students repeat chorally, then in pairs, focusing on natural delivery without pronouncing the silent letter.

periods.teacher_notes: The talk describes rice as a type of grass whose seed we eat — a detail students often find surprising and which provides a useful anchor for the sequencing task. Students commonly place ‘irrigation’ before ‘transplanting’ in the sequence; remind them that the field is flooded specifically to receive transplanted seedlings. For the silent-letter practice, encourage students to say each word in a natural phrase rather than in isolation, since isolated articulation can introduce an unwanted schwa.
materials: Textbook p.181–182 (Let us listen, Let us speak)

periods.activity_title: Harvest Festival Presentation and Farmers’ Slogan

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.182): group presentation on a popular harvest festival dish from your region.
Let us write (p.183): draft a creative slogan expressing gratitude to farmers for the school notice board.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the speaking task (p.182) and groups of four are formed. Each group quickly decides which harvest festival dish to present, using the six prompt questions (name, other names, ingredients, preparation, serving, taste, ritual, memory) as a planning checklist.

Groups plan and deliver their presentations in turn; each group speaks for an unhurried two-to-three minutes. Listeners note one ingredient and one ritual mentioned by each group. Teacher gives brief spoken feedback on clarity and use of descriptive language.

Students move to the slogan-writing task (p.183): teacher models one slogan aloud, noting the three principles — main idea, simple language, conciseness. Students draft, refine, and write their final slogan individually; two or three are shared aloud at the close.

periods.teacher_notes: The group presentation draws on the theme of harvest celebration that runs through the poem — connecting the farmers’ real dishes to the community gratitude expressed in the hymn enriches both activities. For the slogan task, students often write full sentences rather than concise phrases; asking them to count their words and aim for under ten helps sharpen the writing. Encourage quieter students to speak during the presentation planning phase, not only during delivery.
materials: Textbook p.182–183 (Let us speak, Let us write)
Chart paper and markers (optional, for displaying slogans)

periods.activity_title: Millets, Harvest Songs and Community Inquiry

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.184): group inquiry — find out if millets feature in your cuisine and plan a millet recipe.
Let us explore (p.184): share a harvest festival song learned from elders; contribute a verse to a class songbook.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the millet text (p.184) on Pearl Millet and reads it aloud. Students note that millets are small-seeded grasses richer in fibre and minerals than common cereals.

Groups of four take up the millet inquiry task (p.184): they discuss whether millets feature in their home cuisine, brainstorm a recipe they could create, and record both the dish name and its key ingredients on paper. One group member drafts the recipe steps while others note regional millet dishes they know.

Each student shares one or two lines of a harvest festival song they know — learned from family members or from their own cultural tradition (p.184). The class contributes these lines to a collective songbook page drafted on the board or chart paper.

Brief whole-class sharing: groups present their millet recipe to the class in three sentences. Teacher closes by connecting the songs and the recipes to the hymn’s vision of harvest as a celebration of community, land, and gratitude.

periods.teacher_notes: The millet inquiry task connects the poem’s reverence for the earth’s bounty to contemporary nutritional and agricultural awareness, making the beyond-text work genuinely interdisciplinary. Students who do not know a harvest festival song should be encouraged to contribute any song connected to seasons, food, or gratitude from their own tradition. The recipe and song contributions together can constitute a class booklet assembled after this sitting with the teacher’s help.

items.source_context: Four-stanza devotional hymn; Surya, Varuna, Prithvi, Brahma; anaphora, imagery, metaphor, personification; Seed and Scythe; community harvest celebration.
items.item_stem: Read the lines on page 173 beginning “Thine is the bounty that prospered”. Which statement best describes what the repeated phrase ‘Thine is’ at the beginning of successive lines achieves in the poem?

options.label: A
options.text: It creates a sense of confusion by mixing different deities together.

options.label: B
options.text: It builds a litany-like rhythm that reinforces the community’s collective devotion.

options.label: C
options.text: It shows that the farmers are uncertain about which god to address.

options.label: D
options.text: It introduces a new deity in each line of the stanza.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Suggests the student has not recognised anaphora as a structuring device and reads the repetition as disorder.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Indicates a misreading of the devotional tone — the repeated attribution is confident gratitude, not uncertainty.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses the function of the anaphoric phrase with a cataloguing of deities across lines rather than within stanzas.

items.source_lo: Student identifies main ideas, analyses poetic devices, and interprets symbolic meaning using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Four-stanza devotional hymn; Surya, Varuna, Prithvi, Brahma; anaphora, imagery, metaphor, personification; Seed and Scythe; community harvest celebration.
items.item_stem: In the final stanza of ‘Harvest Hymn’, Brahma is called both “the Seed and the Scythe of our harvests” (page 175). Explain what this metaphor reveals about the poet’s understanding of Brahma’s role in creation and in the lives of the farming community. Support your answer with evidence from the poem.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The metaphor presents Brahma as both the origin of life (Seed — the beginning of growth and creation) and its conclusion (Scythe — the reaping that ends the agricultural cycle), embodying the Hindu concept of the divine as the source and end of all existence. This dual role explains why all voices join together in the final stanza to offer their lives and labours as tribute.

items.item_stem: Listen to the talk about paddy cultivation (page 203). Number the following stages in the correct order in which they occur, from first to last.
items.visual_stimulus:
Stage|Order Number
Puddling of land|
Transplanting of seedlings|
Threshing of grains|
Sowing seeds on the soil surface|
Milling of rice|
Harvesting of paddy|

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. Puddling of land
2. Sowing seeds on the soil surface
3. Transplanting of seedlings
4. Harvesting of paddy
5. Threshing of grains
6. Milling of rice

items.source_context: Informational talk on paddy cultivation: ploughing, puddling, sowing, transplanting, irrigating, harvesting, threshing, milling; rice as grass seed.
items.item_stem: Based on the paddy cultivation talk (page 203), why is drying the rice grains after threshing an important step? Choose the correct answer.

options.label: A
options.text: To separate the outer husk from the rice using heat.

options.label: B
options.text: To reduce moisture content so the grains can be stored or processed further.

options.label: C
options.text: To make the grains soft enough to be transplanted in the nursery bed.

options.label: D
options.text: To prepare the grains for sowing in the flooded field.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses drying with milling — the outer covering is removed during milling, not through drying.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Mixes up the post-harvest stage with the pre-transplanting seedling stage.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Misplaces drying in the sequence, placing it before sowing rather than after threshing.

items.item_stem: Sarojini Naidu’s ‘Harvest Hymn’ expresses the farming community’s deep gratitude to the forces of nature that sustain their harvest. Write a short paragraph (80–100 words) from the perspective of a farmer who has just completed the harvest, addressed to future readers of a community journal, explaining what the harvest means to your family and why you feel grateful.

expected_elements: Written in first person from a farmer’s perspective.
Conveys personal meaning of harvest — labour, sustenance, family.
Expresses gratitude to nature or community with specific detail.
Appropriate register for a community journal; within word limit.

items.item_stem: The poem ‘Harvest Hymn’ is written in an archaic register. Rewrite the following lines from the poem using modern English equivalents for the underlined archaic words (thee, thine, thou, hail). Then write one sentence explaining how the change in language affects the tone of the hymn.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Thee = you; thine = your; thou = you; hail = greet or honour. For example, ‘We praise you, O Surya’ and ‘Your is the bounty’. The modern versions sound more casual and lose the elevated, reverent quality of the original, which relies on archaic pronouns to create the solemnity of a formal hymn.

items.item_stem: Sarojini Naidu’s ‘Harvest Hymn’ celebrates the earth’s bounty, including the grains that sustain communities. Millets are one such grain grown across India. Research ONE millet crop grown in your region. In your response, name the millet, describe where it is grown, state two nutritional benefits it offers, and explain how it is used in one traditional dish from your area.

expected_elements: Names a specific millet and its growing region in India.
States two accurate nutritional benefits (fibre, minerals, etc.).
Describes a traditional dish using the millet with some preparation detail.
Connects the millet’s role to the poem’s theme of earth’s nourishing bounty.

items.item_stem: Harvest songs are part of India’s cultural heritage, just as ‘Harvest Hymn’ is a literary expression of that tradition. For a class project: (i) Talk to an elder in your family or community and learn one song sung during a harvest festival. (ii) Write out the song in its original language and provide a short summary in English of what the song expresses. (iii) Explain in three to four sentences how the feelings or themes in the song compare with those in Sarojini Naidu’s poem.

expected_elements: Provides a harvest song sourced from a family or community elder.
Includes an English summary of the song’s meaning or message.
Makes a clear comparison of themes with ‘Harvest Hymn’ (gratitude, nature, community).
Written in complete sentences with accurate spelling and punctuation.
